extracted.intended_audience: appellate attorneys, trial lawyers, and pro se litigants handling federal tax wrongful-disclosure (26 U.S.C. §6103/§7431) claims and related injunction/certiorari practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for litigating wrongful disclosure claims under 26 U.S.C. §6103 and §7431 (including summary judgment, injunctive relief, notice-of-deficiency rules, and appellate/certiorari timeliness). Also covers when disclosures are authorized for collection and the good-faith/no-liability defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary-judgment review standard
rubrics_metrics.description: We review de novo the district court's grant of summary judgment. Viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, the court must determine whether there are any genuine issues of material fact and whether the district court correctly applied the relevant law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate whether summary judgment was appropriate; citations: Kruso v. Int'l Tel. & Tel. Corp., Alaska Airlines v. United Airlines. If no genuine issue of material fact and law applied correctly, affirm. (Text shows the appellate panel applied de novo review and affirmed where disclosures were authorized and no bad-faith evidence existed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and private cause of action under §6103/§7431
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6103 provides that income tax returns and return information are confidential. Section 7431 provides a civil cause of action for damages for the intentional or negligent disclosure of confidential return information by officers or employees of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the substantive basis for a wrongful-disclosure claim; determine whether a disclosure falls within §6103 confidentiality and then whether an exception or authorization applies (e.g., §6103(k)(6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: §6103(k)(6) collection-activity exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6103(k)(6) authorizes the IRS to disclose return information 'in connection with ... any audit, collection activity, or civil or criminal tax investigation' to the extent necessary for collection/enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures made to locate assets, verify financial status, establish liens, levy, seize or sell assets to satisfy liability are authorized. If disclosure was part of authorized collection activity, it is not an unauthorized disclosure under §7431. (Cited cases: Maisano; Hughes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treasury regulation on collection disclosures (§301.6103(k)(6)-1(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal regulations allow disclosures to: 'establish or verify the financial status or condition and location of the taxpayer ..., to locate assets in which the taxpayer has an interest, to ascertain the amount of any liability ... or otherwise to apply the provisions of the Code relating to establishment of liens against such assets, or levy on, or seizure, or sale of, the assets to satisfy any such liability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an IRS action (e.g., recording a federal tax lien, issuing a notice of sale or levy) is taken to collect a tax liability, these regs often make such disclosures lawful. Assess whether the factual disclosures fall within the listed collection purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith/no-liability defense under §7431(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: No liability shall arise under §7431 with respect to any disclosure which results from 'a good faith, but erroneous, interpretation of section 6103.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government may avoid liability by showing disclosures were made in good faith under a (possibly erroneous) interpretation of §6103. Conversely, 'bad faith' is an element the plaintiff must plead and ultimately prove; plaintiffs must plead sufficient facts to establish bad faith (Davidson v. Brady). Lack of evidence of bad faith supports summary judgment for government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for §7431 actions (two-year discovery rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7431(d) provides that an action under §7431(a) must be brought 'within 2 years after the date of discovery by the plaintiff of the unauthorized disclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is a threshold jurisdictional/merits issue; courts dismiss suits filed more than two years after discovery of the allegedly unauthorized disclosure. Determine date of discovery for each alleged disclosure (mail receipt, publication date, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of notice of deficiency (last known address rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of deficiency is valid if it is mailed to the taxpayer's last known address, even if it is never received by the taxpayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal certification (e.g., Form 3624, certified-mail list) or a postal form showing mailing is sufficient, in the absence of contrary evidence, to establish proper mailing (Williams v. Commissioner; Zolla). This affects whether subsequent assessments/collection steps were lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal evidence sufficiency for establishing mailing
rubrics_metrics.description: A postal form certifying that a notice of deficiency has been mailed is sufficient, in the absence of contrary evidence, to establish that the notice was properly mailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts treat certified-mail lists, certified mail numbers, and returned envelopes (e.g., 'unclaimed') as strong evidence the IRS properly mailed the notice. Plaintiffs must produce contrary evidence to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Injunction Act and Enochs judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anti-Injunction Act, 26 U.S.C. §7421(a), prohibits a taxpayer from bringing a suit to restrain assessment or collection of any tax. Under the judicial exception in Enochs v. Williams Packing, injunctive relief is available only if: (1) under no circumstances could the government prevail, and (2) the taxpayer will be irreparably harmed if the injunction is not granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts strictly enforce §7421(a); taxpayers seeking injunctions must satisfy the demanding two-part Enochs test. Financial hardship alone ordinarily does not constitute irreparable harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6213 timing rule and narrow injunctive carve-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6213 provides that no assessment shall be made and no collection proceeding begin until 90 days after mailing of a notice of deficiency; 'notwithstanding the provisions of section 7421(a), ... the making of such assessment ... may be enjoined by a proceeding in the proper court.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the government assessed or began collection during the 90-day period after a properly mailed notice of deficiency, §6213 provides a statutory basis to enjoin; but validity of mailing still controls. Courts consider whether notice was mailed to last known address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized filing of notice of federal tax lien and levies (§6323(f), §6331)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6323(f) and §6331 (and implementing regs) expressly authorize filing of a notice of tax lien in county offices and permit levies to collect unpaid taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a Notice of Federal Tax Lien (Form 668) identifying the taxpayer, liability and assessment date is an authorized collection disclosure; such filings are often deemed authorized disclosures under §6103(k)(6) and related regs, insulating the government from §7431 liability for those particular disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No collateral attack on validity of assessment within a §7431 action
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff may not obtain a judicial determination of the validity of the assessment in the context of a §7431 unlawful disclosure action; the propriety of the underlying assessment generally cannot be collaterally challenged in a §7431 suit (Elias v. Connett).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a §7431 suit is brought, courts will not permit the plaintiff to relitigate assessment validity in that forum; separate statutory remedies (e.g., refund suits) or procedures are the proper vehicles to challenge assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate handling of preliminary injunctive hearing consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court that consolidates a preliminary injunction hearing with the trial on the merits must still address all merits-based factual contentions (e.g., whether an assessment was ever made).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry of judgment following consolidation should be careful to resolve—on the merits—any disputed factual predicate that could support a wrongful-disclosure claim; failure to address a material factual gap (e.g., lack of evidence of assessment) can require remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court certiorari timeliness and rehearing tolling (28 U.S.C. §2101(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for certiorari in a civil case must be filed within 90 days of the entry of the judgment below (28 U.S.C. §2101(c)). A petition for rehearing in the court of appeals generally tolls the 90-day period while it is pending; however, if the court of appeals withdraws or revises an opinion without changing the underlying judgment, the mere revision does not necessarily toll the certiorari period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the court of appeals' actions changed the judgment (tolling) or merely revised the opinion (no toll). If the original judgment remained in effect, certiorari timing runs from entry of that judgment and the 90-day limit is jurisdictional.
